title: Creator-Led Growth Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures whether your distribution is building pipeline or a list of spectators.

questions.text: When you look at who actually engages with your content or creator campaigns, how well do they match your target buyer?

answers.label: Most engagement comes from people with no buying intent — curious, but not buyers
Some buyers are in there but we are not tracking it consistently
We estimate 20 to 30 percent are ICP — gut feel, no hard data
We check engagement demographics against our ICP after each campaign
More than half of engaged accounts match our ICP and we have data to back it

questions.text: How do you decide which creators to partner with for a campaign?

answers.label: Follower count and general topic fit — biggest audience we can afford
Reach and engagement rates within our content category
Audience demographics, but mostly gut feel on whether they fit our buyer
We filter for creators whose specific audience overlaps with our buyer profile before any conversation
We require audience data before signing and score every creator against a written ICP brief

questions.text: After a creator campaign ends, what is the first number you look at to call it a success or a miss?

answers.label: Views, impressions, or follower growth
Clicks and website traffic
Total signups or trials generated
Trial-to-paid conversion rate from that specific campaign
Revenue attributed to the campaign with CAC tracked back to the individual creator

low.headline: Reach without the right buyers is just a bigger list of spectators.
low.text: LinkedIn rewards you by showing your next post to more of whoever already engaged. If that group is not your buyer, more spend just reaches more spectators. A creator with 30K followers whose audience is 70 percent your ICP will outperform one with 200K followers who only loosely fit. The filter is what is missing, and no budget increase fixes that.
steps: Pull the last 90 days of campaign engagement and tag each account as ICP or not — be honest about the actual percentage
Write a one-page ICP brief before the next creator partnership: job title, company size, and the specific pain they search before they find you
Score every creator candidate against that brief and pass on any whose audience overlap is below 25 percent regardless of their reach

mid.headline: You are past vanity metrics. The selection filter still has gaps.
mid.text: You are tracking the right signals, which puts you ahead of most teams in this space. The gap is that creator selection still has gut feel in it. Micro-communities convert better than large audiences because the trust is already built inside them — but that only works when the ICP filter is applied every time, not just when you have bandwidth to check.
steps: Break conversion rate by individual creator — find which audience types actually buy, not just click
Add one ICP-fit question to your creator vetting call: ask them to describe who their top 20 percent most engaged followers are
Set a hard threshold and stick to it: if less than 30 percent of a creator's audience matches your buyer profile, do not run regardless of reach

high.headline: You are thinking in pipelines, not follower counts.
high.text: You have already skipped the failure mode that stalls most teams. The next move is making the process faster and repeatable so it runs at scale without losing the standard you have built. What you do intuitively needs to be written down before it becomes a bottleneck.
steps: Turn your ICP-fit criteria into a one-page creator scorecard your team can run without you in the room
Test one niche channel this quarter — a Discord, Slack group, or industry newsletter — where your exact buyer already talks
Track revenue attribution by individual creator for every active deal and build a ranked list that informs future spend before intuition does

questions.text: If a prospect opened your last outreach DM or cold email right now, how quickly would they know the specific problem you solve for them?

answers.label: It would take a few back-and-forths — the first message is about starting a conversation
The problem is in there but buried in the second or third paragraph
It is in the first paragraph alongside some context about us
The first two sentences name their problem and what we do about it
The subject line or opening line calls out their exact situation — they know within five seconds

questions.text: How specific is your creator campaign brief about what action you want the audience to take?

answers.label: The brief is mainly about brand vibe, tone, and authentic integration
We have a general CTA but leave the details to the creator
We specify the CTA but not the exact offer, pain point, or hook
We brief the specific offer, the exact CTA, and the audience pain to address
We script the trust handoff from creator to product, review drafts before publish, and require a single clear action from the audience

questions.text: When a creator campaign underperforms, what is the first thing you change?

answers.label: Increase the budget or add more creators to recover the volume
Try different creators or shift to a different channel
Rewrite the creative or test a different hook
Audit each funnel step to find exactly where the drop-off happened
Check the trust handoff first — did the creator's audience have a clear reason to act, or did we arrive as a stranger to them?

questions.text: How many hours per week does your team currently spend on manual outreach — writing DMs, emails, and follow-ups by hand?
questions.hint: Count time spent writing, personalizing, and sending. Do not count time inside tools that automate those tasks.

low.headline: Vague pitches go straight to archive. No one buys from a fog machine.
low.text: If your first message cannot answer in the first two lines what problem you solve for this specific person, why you and not the next option, and what is in it for them concretely, you are filling inboxes. The same goes for creator briefs: if the brief is all collaboration and no concrete value, your conversion rate will show it. Clarity and proof and relevance — that is the whole job.
steps: Rewrite your current outreach template so the first two sentences answer: what problem, why you, what they get — then delete everything before those two sentences
Add a so-what test to every campaign brief before it goes to the creator: if you cannot state the audience's specific pain in one sentence, the brief is not ready
Pull the last 10 outreach messages you sent and count how many named a specific problem in the opening line — use that number as your baseline

mid.headline: The structure is right. The specificity still needs work.
mid.text: You have clarity in the brief but the details are still general enough that the right person does not fully recognize themselves. Relevance is about how precisely you describe their situation. A broad descriptor like 'growing AI companies' is not a problem statement. The exact role, the specific trigger, and the concrete cost — that is what gets a reply.
steps: Replace any descriptor like 'growing brands' or 'AI companies' in your outreach with the exact role, company size, and buying trigger you are responding to
Add one concrete proof point to your opening — a result, a number, or a direct reference to something specific about them or their business
Build a brief template that requires the creator to name one specific audience pain before any copy is written — make it a required field, not a suggestion

high.headline: You lead with clarity. Now build the process so it scales.
high.text: Most teams spend months on campaigns that never name the problem. You have already skipped that. The next step is turning what you do well into something repeatable that runs at higher volume without losing the specificity that makes it work.
steps: Document your current briefing format as a reusable template your team can own and run without you in the room
Build a swipe file of your highest-converting outreach openings so the pattern is teachable to the next person who writes one
Test one brief variation where you give the creator a specific audience pain line to open with — track whether it moves the click-to-signup rate and keep the winner

questions.text: What does your landing page assume about a visitor arriving from a creator's video or post?

answers.label: The same as any other visitor — one page, same message for everyone
We have a generic intro paragraph explaining what we do
We acknowledge creator traffic but the rest of the page is untailored
We have a creator-specific page that opens with the audience's pain, not our product features
We test creator-specific pages per campaign and iterate based on what that audience already heard from the creator

questions.text: After someone signs up for your trial, how quickly do they reach the first moment where your product actually makes sense to them?

answers.label: We have not mapped this — they explore on their own after signup
Most users need multiple sessions before they understand what the product does for them
We have onboarding emails but we are not sure how many users actually reach the key moment
We have an activation flow built around one specific moment and we track whether users hit it
We know the exact action that predicts retention and we build the first session around reaching it

questions.text: A creator video sends 5,000 visitors to your site and under 2 percent complete signup. What do you do first?

answers.label: Find a bigger creator to recover the volume
Rebrief the creator with a different hook or creative angle
Cut signup form fields and retest the flow
Map the drop-off across all four stages: click rate, landing page conversion, signup completion, first activation
Fix the funnel before buying more traffic — the same budget through a fixed conversion beats more spend into the same leak

questions.text: What percentage of trial signups from creator campaigns convert to paid within 30 days?
questions.hint: If you track this separately from other traffic sources, use that number. Otherwise use your overall trial-to-paid rate as an estimate.

questions.text: What is your current monthly spend on creator campaigns and paid distribution combined? (USD)
questions.hint: Include creator fees, ad spend, and any paid amplification of creator content.

low.headline: More traffic will not fix a leaky funnel. It makes the leak more expensive.
low.text: Across 100-plus paid creator campaigns, the drop-off happens in the same four places every time: the trust handoff from creator to product, a landing page written for people who already know what you do, signup friction, and the gap between signing up and the moment the product actually clicks. Buying more attention before addressing these is how CAC climbs with nothing to show for it. The team that fixed their landing page and trial flow first got 80 percent of video visitors into the paid plan on the same budget.
steps: Map your funnel as four stages and find where the biggest drop is: click rate from creator content, landing page to signup start, signup completion, signup to first activation
Rewrite your landing page assuming the visitor knows nothing about your product beyond what the creator said in their video
Count the fields in your signup form and remove every one that is not required to reach the first value moment — every field costs you conversions

mid.headline: You are tracking the funnel. Close the gaps you already know about.
mid.text: You are past the stage of ignoring conversion data, which is the first real step most teams skip. The next move is getting specific about the activation moment. A churned trial is a worse outcome than no trial — it burns the creator's trust with their own audience and makes the next campaign harder to pitch.
steps: Define your activation event: the one action that, if taken in the first session, predicts the user stays past day 7
Build a sequence that moves new signups toward that action immediately — a specific instruction, not a welcome email
Track activation rate by traffic source and compare creator traffic to direct — the gap tells you exactly how warm your creator trust handoff really is

high.headline: Your funnel works. Stress-test it at higher volume.
high.text: You have done what most teams avoid: fixed the leak before buying more attention. The question at this stage is whether the funnel holds when campaign volume doubles. Activation flows break at scale in ways they do not at low volume, and the best time to find that ceiling is before you commit to a larger spend.
steps: Run a higher-volume campaign and check whether the trial-to-paid rate holds or drops — find the ceiling before assuming it does not exist
Build a creator-specific onboarding path that references the exact pain the creator named in their content — the trust they built compounds when the product experience continues it
Set a monthly funnel audit: flag any stage that drops more than five points month over month and investigate before increasing spend

questions.text: How often do you reach back out to past customers or churned trials with something genuinely relevant to them?

answers.label: Rarely — we are focused on new acquisition and barely touch the existing list
We send a re-engagement email when we remember or when something new launches
We have an automated win-back sequence but have not checked whether the content is still relevant
We track why trials churned and follow up within 30 days with something specific to their reason for leaving
We run a full lifecycle: a check-in at day 30, a follow-up at day 90, and product tips tied to their actual use case

questions.text: How would you describe your monetization engine right now?

answers.label: We are still figuring out where most of our revenue comes from
We have one primary stream but it is not consistent or predictable
We have a primary stream that works and one or two others we are testing
We have a ranked set of streams — we know which converts best for our specific audience
We have a defined primary engine plus supporting streams, each matched to what our audience naturally buys next

questions.text: If your main creator or paid distribution channel stopped working tomorrow, how much of your audience could you still reach directly?

answers.label: Very little — almost all traffic depends on paid or creator-driven sources
We have a small email list but it is cold and we have not emailed them in months
We have a list we could activate but it would take a few weeks to re-engage them
We have a warm list we could send something to this week and get replies
Owned channels are our first distribution layer — creator and paid sources amplify what already converts

low.headline: You have a follow-up problem, not a lead-gen problem.
low.text: Most businesses keep collecting customer data and then do nothing with it. The people who already bought, or started a trial and left, already fit your ICP, have heard of you, and had a reason to try. Small, consistent contact is how you stay in their memory: a birthday message, a post-purchase tip, a check-in six months later. One saved date, one written template, one automated send. The brands people come back to are the ones that kept showing up with something relevant.
steps: Pull your churned trial list from the last 6 months and count how many you have followed up with something specific to why they left — not a discount, something that addresses the actual gap
Set up one automated post-trial sequence: a check-in at day 7, a resource tied to their use case at day 30, and a follow-up at day 90 with a new feature or relevant result
Pick one owned channel — email, community, or newsletter — and commit to a monthly send before adding any new acquisition spend

mid.headline: You are touching the right channels. The depth is still missing.
mid.text: You have built the infrastructure. The gap is relevance. Generic re-engagement emails get the same response as generic cold outreach. Every touchpoint needs to be tied to something specific about that person's situation — what they tried, what they did not finish, or what they purchased six months ago. That specificity is the difference between a brand that feels present and one that feels like spam.
steps: Segment your list by product behavior — what they activated and where they churned — and build separate sequences for each segment rather than one message for everyone
Add one behavioral trigger to your win-back flow: if a churned user visits your pricing page again, follow up within 24 hours with something specific to where they dropped off
Map your monetization streams by conversion rate and put more behind the one that closes fastest for your actual audience type — the business model wins every time

high.headline: You have built the engine most teams are still trying to describe.
high.text: Owned distribution, a ranked monetization model, and a lifecycle that does not depend on what the algorithm decides tomorrow. The next phase is using what retention data tells you about your best customers to sharpen how you acquire, not just how you keep.
steps: Feed your best-retained customer profiles back into your creator selection criteria — the audience that activates and stays is the audience worth paying to reach
Build one referral or community mechanism that turns your retained customers into a distribution channel on their own
Review your monetization stack against your top 20 percent of customers and ask: what is their next natural buy that you are not currently offering?

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
